messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: user-supplied baseline model
parts:
Hello Yves,

I'd like to suggest the addition of a new argument to the lavaan function that would allow the user to override the default baseline model (perhaps similar to the slotParTable argument).  In multiple-group and longitudinal models, a more restrictive baseline model may be more appropriate for calculating incremental fit indices than the traditional independence model, which allows variances/means of variables to differ across groups/occasions.  Or in the case of latent growth curve models, a common constraint (although often an unnecessary one) is to constrain the residual variances to equality over time.  In such a case, the traditional independence model is not nested within the (albeit less restrictive) hypothesized model, so it is not an appropriate baseline model for calculating CFI.  Bentler & Satorra's (2010) Nesting/Equivalence Testing method can verify this, using the code below.

Thank you for all your work on lavaan!

Terry



growthModel <- '
# intercept and slope with fixed coefficients
i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4
t1 ~~ e*t1
t2 ~~ e*t2
t3 ~~ e*t3
t4 ~~ e*t4
'

growthFit <- growth(growthModel, data = Demo.growth)
summary(growthFit, fit = TRUE)


baselineModel <- '
t1 ~~ t1
t2 ~~ t2
t3 ~~ t3
t4 ~~ t4
t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 ~ 1
'
baseFit <- growth(baselineModel, data = Demo.growth)
summary(baseFit, fit = TRUE)


base.sigma <- baseFit@Fi...@Sigma.hat[[1]]
base.mu <- as.numeric(baseFit@Fi...@Mu.hat[[1]])
rownames(base.sigma) <- paste0("t", 1:4)
colnames(base.sigma) <- paste0("t", 1:4)
names(base.mu) <- paste0("t", 1:4)
base.sigma
base.mu

## if the baseModel were nested within the growthModel, its model-implied
## moments could be perfectly reproduced by the growthModel (i.e., chi-sq = 0)
nestedTest <- growth(growthModel, sample.cov = base.sigma, sample.mean = base.mu,
                     std.lv = TRUE, sample.nobs = nrow(Demo.growth))
summary(nestedTest, fit = TRUE)

Thanks, Yves!

For any other interested readers, I read about another common reason to need to specify a manual baseline model -- When we fit a model to incomplete data using FIML, and we include auxiliary variables using the saturated correlates approach, we need to make sure the auxiliaries are saturated in the baseline model as well.

Regarding the growth model in my first post, I haven't been able to specify a baseline model that IS nested within a hypothesized model whose residual variances are constrained to equality.  I think this is because the mean structure is a linear growth pattern in the hypothesized model, but even when I specify all means to be equal (i.e., an intercept-only model) and all variances to be equal (corresponding to the constrained residual variances, I believe), the baseline model is not nested within the hypothesized model.  Does anyone has any insight or citations on this baseline models for latent growth curves?

Thanks,

Terry

Scratch that, I made a syntax error.  The intercept-only (same means, same variances) model is nested within the growth curve with restricted residual variances.  Thanks to Alex for reminding me about some citations, for interested parties:

Wu, W., West, S. G., & Taylor, A. B. (2009). Evaluating model fit for growth curve models: integration of fit indices from SEM and MLM frameworks. Psychological Methods, 14, 183-201.

Wu, W., & West, S. G. (2010): Sensitivity of Fit Indices to Misspecification in Growth Curve Models, Multivariate Behavioral Research, 45(3), 420-452.

Widamin, K. F., & Thompson, J. S. (2003). On Specifying the Null Model for Incremental Fit Indices in Structural Equation Modeling. Psychological Methods, 8(1), 16-37.

messages.subject: Re: user-supplied baseline model
parts:
Yes, this has been on my TODO list for a looong time (I believe since my
last visit in Kansas). Will bump it up.

Yves,

I was wondering where in the lavaan object you stored information about the baseline model, thinking maybe there was something I could customize with update().  But I saw in lav_fit_measures.R and 10lavaan-methods.R that you don't run the baseline model until it is requested in a call to summary(), inspect(), or fitMeasures().  That gave me an idea for a quick and easy update to fitMeasures() that would allow users to specify a custom baseline model.

Rather than specifying syntax in a call to lavaan() --- which I originally thought would be easier only because I thought the lavaan object contained baseline-model information --- the user would actually fit their custom baseline model in a separate call to lavaan(), then pass that fitted lavaan object to fitMeasures().  I made a copy of this function, and the only changes I made were to add a new argument (with a default NULL value):

fitMeasures <- fitmeasures <- function(object, fit.measures = "all", baseFit = NULL) {

and to change this line (currently line 246 on github)

fit.indep <- independence.model.fit(object)

to these lines

if (!is.null(baseFit) & is(baseFit, "lavaan")) {
  fit.indep <- baseFit
} else {
  fit.indep <- independence.model.fit(object)
}

and it appears to work fine.  I didn't look too deeply into the internals of lavaan, so I might be missing some subtleties.

It would be very convenient for users to supply baseline-model syntax, but this small change might be easier to implement (although it looks like you may have started working on that just above line 246 in lav_fit_measures.R).  It would certainly not be hard for users to take the extra step to fit custom baseline-model syntax to data and pass the resulting fitted object to fitMeasures() instead of passing the syntax itself.  Of course, the user-specified baseline model couldn't be passed to summary() or inspect() unless new arguments were added there as well, and that might be more complicated, especially if you want to allow arguments for modificationIndices() or standardizedSolution() to be passed to inspect() as well.

Anyway, I was thinking of making the simple edit on github, but I didn't know if you wanted users suggesting changes that way.  Regardless of your decision, thank you for all your work on lavaan.

Terry

Dear Yves and Terry,
I am quite interested by this thread as I am fitting sem models for interchangeable dyads (e.g. twins). In the following paper, they show how to specify proper null and saturated models for this type of data as well as how to correct chi-square and indices. Being able to specify a null model AND a saturated model would be very useful to get directly the modified chi square and fit indices. So please, keep us posted of your work! Thanks a lot!
JB
Here is the ref: Olsen and Kenny, SEM with interchangeable dyads, Psychological Methods, 2006, Vol. 11, No. 2, 127–141.
